explain.say: South of the Sahara lies a long strip of dry grassland called the Sahel, stretching more than 5,000 kilometres from Senegal to Sudan. Sahel means shore: the edge of the desert. Look at the board. This circle shows how good land can slowly turn into desert, and keep getting worse.

explain.say: It often begins with drought, which means a long time with too little rain. In the 1970s and 1980s, the Sahel had terrible droughts. Crops failed and the grass dried up. What do you think hungry animals eat when the grass runs out?

explain.say: Next, the plants are removed. Goats and cattle eat every last leaf, which is called overgrazing, and families cut trees for cooking fires. Now see the bare soil: with no roots to hold it, it bakes hard. Can you see the circle starting to turn?

explain.say: Then wind and rare storms strip away the topsoil, the rich top layer where plants grow. Bare land soaks up less rain, so even fewer plants grow, and the circle spins again. This is called desertification. Why do you think it is called a vicious circle?

explain.say: But people are breaking the circle! In Burkina Faso, farmers dig small pits called zaï to catch rain, and in Niger farmers let tree stumps regrow, greening millions of hectares. Fantastic thinking! Wow fact: African countries are building the Great Green Wall, a belt of trees and farms meant to cross the whole continent.

faq.a: The Sahel is a dry belt of grassland and scrub between the Sahara to the north and the savanna to the south. It runs from Senegal and Mauritania to Sudan and Eritrea, and it has one short rainy season a year.
asks: Which countries are in the Sahel?

faq.a: Desertification is dry land losing its plants and soil. It is caused by droughts and a warming climate together with overgrazing, cutting trees and farming that wears out the soil. It is not simply the Sahara moving south.
Yes. Farmers dig zaï pits and build lines of stones to catch rain, let tree stumps regrow, and plant trees among crops. These steps have brought green back to large areas of Niger and Burkina Faso.
asks: How do farmers stop soil blowing away?

faq.q: What is the Great Green Wall?
faq.a: It is an African Union project, launched in 2007, to restore land across the Sahel in a belt about 8,000 km long, from Senegal to Djibouti. It is now a patchwork of trees, farms and grassland rather than one line of trees.
asks: How long is the Great Green Wall?

faq.a: Topsoil is the top layer of soil, usually only a few centimetres to about 30 cm deep. It holds most of the food plants need and most soil life, and it can take hundreds of years to form.

facts: The Great Green Wall was launched by the African Union in 2007 and aims to span about 8,000 km across Africa.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration in Niger has regreened around 5 million hectares of land.
The Sahel suffered severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s.

quiz.say: Goats and cattle eat all the plants until the soil is bare. What is this called?
quiz.show: Animals eating all the plants is called…
quiz.why: Overgrazing means animals eat plants faster than they can grow back.

wrong.2: Deposition means dropping sand or mud, as rivers and waves do.
